title: An introduction to A Level organic chemistry
overview: Extend organic nomenclature to more complex molecules, understand aromatic (benzene) bonding, and optical isomerism. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Use advanced organic nomenclature and recognise functional groups.
Explain benzene bonding and aromatic delocalisation.
Identify chiral centres, enantiomers and optical activity.
Represent 3D stereochemistry and reason about racemic mixtures.

definitions.definition: An aromatic hydrocarbon containing a benzene ring.
Electron density spread over several adjacent atoms rather than confined to one bond.
Usually a tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups.
Rotation of plane-polarised light by a chiral sample.
An equal mixture of two enantiomers with no net optical rotation.

sections.title: Naming complex molecules
content: Choose the parent chain/ring containing the highest-priority functional group, number for the lowest relevant locants, and name substituents alphabetically. Recognise phenyl (C₆H₅–) as a substituent and distinguish benzyl/side-chain positions when structures are supplied.
bullets: The suffix functional group controls the parent and numbering.
Use commas between numbers and hyphens between numbers and words.

examples.label: Key relationship
examples.content: Benzene: C₆H₆: planar σ framework + six delocalised π electrons

sections.title: Benzene structure
content: Each carbon is trigonal planar and contributes one p orbital. Six π electrons are delocalised above and below the planar σ framework, making all C–C bonds equal and the ring more stable than a localised cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene model.
bullets: Use a circle or equal bonds to represent delocalisation.
Aromatic stability helps explain substitution rather than addition.

sections.title: Chirality and enantiomers
content: A carbon with four different substituents is chiral unless symmetry makes the whole molecule achiral. Draw mirror images with wedge/dash bonds and test superimposability. Enantiomers share most physical properties but rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions and may interact differently with chiral reagents.
bullets: A carbon with two identical groups is not chiral.
Do not confuse E/Z isomerism with optical isomerism.

sections.title: Formation and mixtures
content: Attack on a planar intermediate from either face can produce equal enantiomers and a racemic mixture. A single enantiomer may form when a chiral environment, catalyst or starting material differentiates the faces. Connect stereochemical reasoning to the mechanism supplied.
bullets: A racemate contains molecules that are individually chiral.
Zero net rotation results from cancellation, not absence of enantiomers.

formulas.label: Benzene
formulas.expression: C₆H₆: planar σ framework + six delocalised π electrons

formulas.label: Optical cancellation
formulas.expression: equal (+) and (−) rotations ⇒ zero net rotation

diagram.title: An introduction to A Level organic chemistry: revision route

examTips: Circle every potential stereocentre and list its four substituents before deciding.
Use the delocalised model—not alternating isolated double bonds—in explanation questions.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Calling any carbon with four bonds chiral.
Saying electrons are stationary halfway between benzene bonds.
Saying a racemate contains no optically active molecules.

quickRecall.question: What structural feature usually creates chirality?
quickRecall.answer: A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups.

quickRecall.question: Why are benzene C–C bonds equal?
quickRecall.answer: The six π electrons are delocalised around the ring.

quickRecall.question: Why is a racemic mixture optically inactive?
quickRecall.answer: Equal and opposite rotations from the two enantiomers cancel.

quickRecall.question: Are enantiomers structural isomers?
quickRecall.answer: No; they have the same connectivity and are stereoisomers.
